chief_complaint: gradual onset unilateral scrotal pain and swelling with dysuria and relief when lifting scrotum
hpi_details: 24M sexually active male with three days of gradual right scrotal swelling, urethral discharge, relief with scrotal elevation, and hypervascular flow on Doppler ultrasound. The presentation is consistent with epididymitis, but torsion must be considered clinically before treatment is finalized.
ideas: He thinks he picked up a sexually transmitted infection from a new partner that has spread into his right testicle.
concerns: He is worried that the severe swelling will permanently damage his testicle or cause infertility.
expectations: He hopes to receive antibiotics to clear the infection and effective pain medicine so he can make it through his work shift tomorrow.

available_results.value: Enlarged hypervascular right epididymis with preserved symmetric intratesticular arterial flow; no focal abscess

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Epididymo-Orchitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
In younger sexually active men, gonorrhea and chlamydia are common causes; treatment should be guided by sexual exposure history and local/current STI guidance.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: gradual onset unilateral scrotal pain and swelling with dysuria and relief when lifting scrotum
Key HPI features: gradual unilateral swelling, urethral discharge, relief with elevation, and Doppler hypervascularity.
Objective/Exam findings: Examine for focal epididymal tenderness, testicular lie, cremasteric reflex, hernia, and systemic toxicity. Prehn sign is not reliable for excluding torsion.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Epididymo-Orchitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute epididymitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Failing to exclude testicular torsion in a patient with acute scrotal pain; imaging must not delay urgent urologic assessment when torsion is plausible.
Treating presumed STI-associated epididymitis without NAAT testing, partner management, and HIV/syphilis testing.
Missing abscess, infarction, or another diagnosis when severe symptoms persist or do not improve within 72 hours.
management_principles: Obtain urine or urethral NAAT for gonorrhea/chlamydia and test for HIV and syphilis; obtain urine culture when enteric organisms are possible.

For suspected gonorrhea/chlamydia, use current guideline-directed ceftriaxone plus doxycycline after collecting tests when feasible; add enteric coverage only when exposure history supports it and safety/renal factors are reviewed.

Provide NSAID analgesia if safe, rest and scrotal elevation. Advise no sex until the treatment course is complete, symptoms have resolved, and partners have been treated; arrange partner notification and retesting per local STI guidance.
Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: UpToDate & National Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guidelines 2026

reference_soap.subjective: 24M with three days of gradual right scrotal swelling, urethral discharge, and relief with elevation. Clarify suddenness, nausea/vomiting, sexual exposures (including insertive anal sex), fever, urinary symptoms, and trauma.
reference_soap.objective: Assess vital signs and scrotal exam for epididymal tenderness, testicular lie, cremasteric reflex, and hernia. Doppler supports inflammation but does not override urgent clinical concern for torsion.
reference_soap.assessment: Probable sexually transmitted epididymitis; torsion remains an emergency differential if presentation or examination is concerning.
reference_soap.plan: Urgent urology/ED assessment if torsion is possible. Otherwise collect gonorrhea/chlamydia NAAT and appropriate STI tests, then treat using current guideline-directed therapy based on exposure history. Provide analgesia/scrotal support, partner management, abstinence advice, and review within 72 hours if not improving.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Acute Epididymo-Orchitis Chlamydia
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for gradual onset unilateral scrotal pain and swelling with dysuria and relief when lifting scrotum
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for urology
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: Inflammation of the epididymis, sometimes extending to the testis, often caused by sexually transmitted pathogens in younger sexually active men.
red_flags: Sudden severe scrotal pain or a high-riding testis, requiring urgent exclusion of torsion
Fever, systemic toxicity, or suspected abscess

must_ask.say: Did the scrotal pain and swelling develop gradually over several days?
Have you had burning urination, urethral discharge, or recent sexual exposure?
Does gently lifting your scrotum relieve the pain?
Did you suffer any hit or trauma to your groin area before the pain started?
Do you have a fever or burning when you urinate?

history.answer: My right testicle has been swollen and aching for the past three days, and it burns when I pee.
It started about three days ago as a mild ache and has gradually gotten worse. It didn't wake me up suddenly in the middle of the night.
It is only on my right side, mostly behind and above the right testicle.
It's a constant, dull, heavy ache, around a five or six out of ten in severity.
The ache radiates up into my right groin and lower belly, but it does not go to my flank or back.
Yes, when I gently lift or support my scrotum with my hand or wear tight underwear, the pain eases up a bit.
No, I have never had pain or swelling like this before.
No, I haven't had any nausea and I haven't vomited.
The right side has been steadily swollen for three days. Lying down relieves the dragging feeling, but the swelling itself doesn't disappear.
Yes, it feels quite heavy and aches noticeably more when I've been on my feet or walking around for a while.
No, the whole back of the testicle is swollen and tender, not a painless hard lump.
I have a burning pain whenever I pass urine, and I feel like I need to go more frequently.
I noticed a small amount of cloudy discharge from the tip of my penis yesterday morning.
I have felt slightly feverish and warm since yesterday, but I haven't had severe shaking chills.
The skin on the right side of my scrotum looks red and feels warm, but there are no black spots, sores, or foul smell.
No, I haven't had any trauma or injury down there, and it didn't start during heavy lifting or sex.
No, I haven't had any swelling or pain around my cheeks or jaw, and I had all my childhood shots.
Both of my testicles have always been normally situated in the scrotum, and I've never had any groin or testicular surgery.
No unexplained weight loss, back pain, cough, or breast enlargement.
I am sexually active. I had a new female partner about two weeks ago, and we did not use condoms consistently.
No, I have never had a urinary catheter, bladder scope, or prostate procedure.
I am not trying to have children at the moment, and I don't have diabetes or any immune problems.
I thought I probably caught an STI from a new partner that spread into my right testicle.
I'm really worried the swelling is going to kill the testicle or leave me unable to have kids.
I'm hoping to get some antibiotics to knock this out and something for the pain so I can make it through work tomorrow.
I have high blood pressure and mild high cholesterol.
I've never had any operations and I have never been hospitalized.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once a day for my blood pressure. I haven't taken any painkillers yet.
I have no known allergies to any medications.
I do not smoke cigarettes or use tobacco.
I drink socially, maybe one or two beers on the weekend.
I work as a software engineer and live alone in an apartment.
My father has hypertension, but there is no family history of testicular cancer or other urologic problems.

exam.finding: The patient is alert, oriented, and sitting cautiously with mild discomfort, without acute toxic distress.
Blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg, pulse 78 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 99% on ambient air, and temperature 37.5°C.
Abdomen is soft and non-distended, with mild tenderness to deep palpation in the right lower quadrant, but no peritoneal signs.
No visible or palpable inguinal bulge on Valsalva maneuver, and no inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Right hemiscrotum is erythematous and enlarged with exquisite tenderness along the posterior epididymis; the right testis has a normal vertical lie, bilateral cremasteric reflexes are present, and there is no transillumination.
